Sāṅkhyayoga, "the yoga of knowledge," is the Gītā's philosophical hinge: Arjuna has laid down his bow, and Kṛṣṇa spends the whole chapter answering his despair before a single arrow is fired. The teaching moves in three movements. First Kṛṣṇa argues that the self (ātman) that inhabits the body is unborn and undying, untouched by the weapons that can only reach the body it wears, so that grief for the dead or fear of killing rests on a mistake about what a person really is (verses 11–30). He then turns to Arjuna's standing as a kṣatriya, arguing that a warrior has nothing better than a battle fought in a just cause, and that refusing it brings both sin and lasting disgrace (verses 31–38). From there the chapter opens its second and more lasting teaching: action performed without attachment to its fruit, buddhi-yoga, "the yoga of understanding," culminating in the single most quoted verse of the poem, on the right to the act itself but never to its results (verse 47). The chapter closes with a portrait of the sthitaprajña, "the man of steady wisdom," whose senses are drawn in like a tortoise's limbs and whose mind receives the world's desires the way the ocean receives rivers, without being disturbed — ending on the promise that this settled state is itself a share in brahman, reachable even at the hour of death.
